li.a: France 24: At least 160 killed in deadliest attack in Burkina Faso since 2015
CNN: Solhan, Burkina Faso: How children were used in a 48-hour deadly rampage for gold
Al Jazeera: 'Kill them all, don't spare anyone': A massacre in Burkina Faso
GI-TOC Risk Bulletin: Criminal economies are a key factor in Burkina Faso's Solhan massacre
The Organization for World Peace: Solhan Massacre In Burkina Faso
Solace Global: Burkina Faso: Jihadist Attack Kills Over One Hundred Civilians

content.p: In the first days of June 2021, two raids hit villages in Yagha, a province in the north-east of Burkina Faso. The first, on a Friday evening, killed 14 people at Tadaryat. The second, in the small hours that followed, fell on Solhan, a village built around an informal gold-mining site. Officials counted 132 civilian dead. Local officials told AFP at least 160 had died, and estimates quoted by CNN ran from 170 to 200. By any of those figures it was the deadliest single attack in the country since jihadist violence began there in 2015.

Three questions have followed the killings ever since. Who did it, why, and why did soldiers not stop it? No group claimed the attack, the government and independent analysts give different pictures of the motive, and survivors accuse the army of leaving them defenceless. A striking detail made the massacre notorious abroad: witnesses and the government itself said that many of the gunmen were children.

Burkina Faso had been fighting armed groups linked to al-Qaeda and the Islamic State since 2015. AFP counted around 1,400 deaths and more than a million people driven from their homes by June 2021. Al Jazeera, citing the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), reported that after a lull around the November 2020 presidential election, linked to a temporary ceasefire between the government and some armed groups, attacks resumed and spiked, especially against civilians.

The state leaned on a civilian militia, the Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland, known by the French initials VDP. It was created in law in January 2020 and its members get two weeks of training from state security services. AFP counted more than 200 VDP fatalities by June 2021. GI-TOC notes that the militias have themselves been accused of human rights violations.

Solhan, about 15 kilometres from the provincial town of Sebba, had been hit before. Residents told Al Jazeera that the police station was attacked twice at the end of 2019, killing one officer, and that in October 2020 attackers burned down a school and warned teachers and pupils to stay away. Before June 2021, they said, civilians had not been harmed. On 14 May the defence minister had visited Sebba to tell people life was returning to normal.

AFP reported that the attack on Tadaryat, in the same region, killed 14 people, among them an armed volunteer who had come to help the villagers. Solace Global, a risk consultancy, put Tadaryat about 150 kilometres north of Solhan. The Organization for World Peace and Solace Global both describe it as the attack that came just before Solhan. The sources consulted give little further detail on it.

CNN's reconstruction, built on interviews with survivors, local witnesses and officials, many of whom asked for anonymity, begins on the afternoon of 4 June. Boureima Ly, the emir of the Yagha region, told CNN that more than 100 jihadists on dozens of motorbikes and tricycles had been spotted some 20 kilometres from Solhan. According to an activist, Aly Bokoum, the army was told but did not know whether Solhan or nearby Sebba would be the target, so the local unit stayed in Sebba. Bokoum said the VDP in Solhan also contacted the army and was told to leave the village.

The gold sites came first. A mining official and a miner said the Mousiga mines, east of Solhan, were hit before the village. Distant gunfire was mistaken for a routine army patrol, the official said, so some miners stayed by their wells. Witnesses told CNN the first shots in Solhan itself came at 2:08 a.m., at the mines. Miners often sleep outdoors beside their pits, and several described men shot where they lay, others cut down as they climbed out, and others hiding in wells some 30 feet deep. An official said the first person to reach the site the next day described bodies lying "like fish".

A bus assistant, Abdoulaye Diallo, told Al Jazeera that he lay on the roof of a bus in the station car park while attackers killed people below. He said they drove the bus through the village, looting and ordering the destruction of telecom masts, then set it alight. He jumped and ran under fire. Diallo said he heard the attackers radio a commander for orders and receive the reply, "Kill them all, don't spare anyone". Al Jazeera presents this as his account. A former security guard for the mobile phone mast told CNN that the attackers disabled the mast and removed its battery, cutting the village off.

AFP, citing a local source, reported that the assailants struck around 2 a.m. against a VDP position before moving on to homes, where they carried out "executions". In a statement the government said that "terrorists" had killed civilians of every age and burned homes and the main market. Several witnesses told CNN the attackers seemed to know the village layout well.
content.h2: Children and women among the attackers
content.p: Witnesses told CNN the killers included children, some apparently as young as 12, and women who urged them on. A police source said witnesses distinctly heard women's voices directing the others to particular houses and saying nobody could be allowed to leave. Abdou Hoeffi of the Burkina Faso Movement for Human and People's Rights told CNN the women played a cheerleading role, shouting encouragement such as "You are a good shooter!". Not every account agrees: a miner who fled the Mousiga mines said he saw no children in the group that hit his site, and two other officials denied that children were involved there.

GI-TOC says it spoke to four witnesses, all of whom said child soldiers made up most of the assailants, and that a survivor it calls Alassane described his attackers as around 15. It cites a statement from Burkina Faso's communication minister, Ousseni Tamboura, confirming that most of the combatants in Solhan were children, and calls this the first confirmed major use of child soldiers in the country's conflict. It could not establish where or how the children had been recruited. A VDP member told the organisation they were drawn from the local area.
One witness told CNN that attackers took away a shopkeeper and a young boy, and described a breastfeeding infant being carried off.
content.h2: The army, and a second night
content.p: Diallo told Al Jazeera that soldiers arrived at about 6 a.m., fired warning shots in the air and did not pursue the attackers, then left before sunset. CNN's witnesses also said the army came for a few hours in the morning and left before dusk. A survivor, Hama Amadou, told Al Jazeera that the army had been warned of an attack weeks earlier, and that when volunteers phoned for help during the raid they were told to run. Al Jazeera could not verify this. An officer based in Dori, speaking without authorisation, told the outlet that the Sebba detachment received a call that cut out before the volunteers could explain, and said the army had never been warned beforehand. The army did not answer CNN's requests for comment.

According to Diallo, the attackers came back the following night and set about burning the village and taking what remained. CNN heard from witnesses of homes burned down to their roof sheeting, shops emptied of clothes, drink and money, and a charred health clinic. Two officials told CNN the convoy had not truly left at first light but waited in the bush for nightfall. The CNN reporting counts the violence as a 48-hour rampage. More than 7,000 families fled to nearby villages, the Organization for World Peace reported, and the hospital in Dori was described by a police source as overwhelmed.

The first official count, announced by President Kabore, was 138. AFP then reported that local people recovering bodies had pushed the figure to at least 160, including around 20 children, with many buried in mass graves. GI-TOC gives 132 civilians by official figures and at least 160 by local sources. CNN's reporting cites estimates from a local police source and other officials of between 170 and 200 dead. Tamboura later told CNN that the government's figure of 132 included attackers killed in the incident and fatalities from a neighbouring attack. Al Jazeera's survivors said that bodies were still being found in mine shafts weeks later and that the real number was probably higher than documented.

No group claimed the massacre. The Organization for World Peace noted this a fortnight later, and GI-TOC reports that JNIM issued a statement denying responsibility and condemning it. CNN added that an Islamic State-affiliated newspaper blamed al-Qaeda for it.

The government blamed jihadists. Tamboura told Radio France Internationale, as CNN reported, that two suspects had been detained before the attack and that those arrests had led officials to a little-known group he called Mujahed al Qaeda, linked to JNIM. He told CNN in November that the government believed JNIM was behind it. GI-TOC says the group the government named is separate from JNIM and from the Islamic State's Sahel branch, and notes that some analysts doubt it exists. GI-TOC's own assessment was that the available evidence pointed to a group loosely affiliated with JNIM. A French intelligence official told CNN the attackers were probably a group in formation linked to JNIM, while adding that indiscriminate attacks on civilians were more typical of the Islamic State. The suspects in the investigation were described only as detained in the sources consulted, and none of them reports a trial.

On motive the sources split. ACLED's Heni Nsaibia, quoted by Al Jazeera, listed possible factors: efforts to control and cut off the population of Yagha, where some towns had been blockaded for months; revenge on villages that back the volunteer fighters; and weak cohesion inside the al-Qaeda-linked group. GI-TOC says several commentators, including Human Rights Watch, called the massacre vengeance for VDP recruitment at the mine, but argues that the picture is more complex and tied to criminal economies, with armed groups taxing or robbing miners and sometimes working mines themselves. It quotes a Burkinabe analyst who believes the aim was to take control of the mine for profit. CNN reported that Tamboura told RFI gold was also a motivating factor, and that he later said the jihadist groups were fuelled by hunger to control resources rather than by ideology. CNN itself noted that few officials or witnesses agreed on a single coherent motive.

The government declared three days of national mourning. Kabore called the massacre "barbaric" and "despicable". The UN chief, Antonio Guterres, through his spokesman, said he was outraged, and Pope Francis prayed for the victims after the Angelus. Authorities halted gold mining in Yagha and banned motorcycles, the main transport of the attackers, according to the Organization for World Peace; GI-TOC reports that artisanal mines across the province were closed and that mining has largely stopped, though some small-scale illegal digging continues.

Protests followed in Dori over the lack of protection, CNN reported. According to Al Jazeera, in July Kabore fired his defence and security ministers and briefly took the defence portfolio himself, and in August the defence ministry announced a revised counterterrorism strategy. CNN reported that the government fired some security personnel in the immediate aftermath. Al Jazeera reported that locals call Solhan a turning point; a sociologist at Joseph Ki-Zerbo University told it that the attack shocked the country and exposed internal operational problems in the military. Diallo said he would not return until the army proved it could protect people. Another survivor told CNN: "As soon as the army left, [the attackers] came again."
